before.content_html:
H.G. Wells & The War of the Worlds

H.G. Wells published The War of the Worlds in 1898, at the height of the British Empire. Wells was not simply writing an adventure story — he used the Martian invasion as a vehicle to critique Victorian society’s arrogance, its faith in science and technology, and its brutal treatment of colonised peoples. The novel asks a devastating question: what would happen if Britain, the world’s greatest imperial power, suddenly became the victim of a superior force?

Wells came from a working-class background in Bromley, Kent. His father was an unsuccessful shopkeeper; his mother a domestic servant. He won a scholarship to the Normal School of Science in London, where he studied biology under Thomas Henry Huxley, a champion of Darwinism. This scientific education profoundly shaped the novel. The Martians are not supernatural — they are a more evolved species applying the same logic of survival that Darwin described. Wells forces his readers to see humanity not as the pinnacle of creation, but as one species among many, vulnerable to extinction.

Wells was also a committed socialist, a member of the Fabian Society alongside George Bernard Shaw. He believed the British class system was unjust and that imperialism was morally indefensible. The War of the Worlds channels these beliefs into fiction: the invasion exposes the fragility of Victorian social structures and forces readers to question whether their comfortable world is as secure as they believe.

Key Fact

Wells critiques three aspects of Victorian society: (1) Imperial arrogance — Britain conquered other nations; now it is conquered. (2) Scientific overconfidence — Victorian technology is useless against the Martians. (3) Social Darwinism — the belief that “superior” races have the right to dominate “inferior” ones is turned against humanity.

The British Empire

By 1898, the British Empire controlled a quarter of the world’s surface and governed over 400 million people. Victorians believed their technological and military superiority gave them the right — even the duty — to colonise other peoples. This attitude was reinforced by Social Darwinism, the idea that some races were naturally “superior” and destined to rule. Wells deliberately reverses this dynamic: the Martians treat humans exactly as the British treated colonised peoples — as inferior beings to be conquered, exploited, and consumed.

The timing of the novel is significant. The 1890s were a period of fin de siècle anxiety — a widespread sense that the century was ending and that change was coming. The Boer War (1899–1902), which began just a year after the novel’s publication, would expose the weaknesses of the British military and shake public confidence in the Empire. Wells anticipated this crisis of confidence.

Wells makes the colonial parallel explicit in the novel’s opening chapter, referencing the destruction of the Tasmanians by European colonisers. He writes: “Before we judge [the Martians] too harshly, we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought, not only upon animals … but upon its inferior races.” The word “inferior” is deliberately loaded — it echoes the language that Victorians used to justify colonisation. By applying it to humanity as a whole, Wells forces his readers to confront the horror of their own imperial logic.

Science & Technology

The late Victorian period was an era of extraordinary scientific progress. Railways, telegraphs, electric lighting, and new weapons gave Victorians confidence that technology could solve any problem and that human progress was unstoppable. Wells subverts this confidence completely. The British military’s best weapons — artillery, warships, even the Thunder Child — are destroyed by the Martians’ Heat-Ray. Technology, which Victorians worshipped as proof of their superiority, proves utterly inadequate against a genuinely superior civilisation.

Wells also draws on real astronomical discoveries. In the 1870s and 1880s, astronomers observed what appeared to be canals on the surface of Mars, sparking speculation about Martian civilisation. The astronomer Percival Lowell published hugely popular books arguing that intelligent beings had built an irrigation system on Mars. Wells takes this speculation and turns it into a nightmare: the Martians are not just intelligent — they are so far ahead of humans that our species is no more significant to them than insects are to us.

Key Fact

Wells references the Tasmanian genocide to draw a direct parallel between the Martian invasion and British imperialism. He forces readers to see the invasion from the perspective of colonised peoples — making the novel a sustained critique of empire, not just an adventure story. This reference appears in the very first chapter, establishing the political argument before the action begins.

For the Eduqas C720U Component 2 Section B exam, you will receive a printed extract from The War of the Worlds and write about both the extract and the wider novel. Context (AO3) is worth up to 10 of the 40 marks. Always link context to Wells’s methods and purpose — don’t just list facts about Victorian science or empire. The strongest responses will show how Wells uses the science fiction genre itself as a method of social critique.

before.content_html:
Book 1: The Coming of the Martians

The novel’s opening is deliberately calm. The narrator describes a quiet evening in Woking, Surrey, as a “falling star” streaks across the sky. Wells establishes the mundane normality of Victorian suburban life before destroying it. The contrast between the ordinary setting and the extraordinary event is crucial — it makes the invasion feel real and immediate.

The cylinder lands on Horsell Common, and curious crowds gather to watch it being unscrewed. Wells presents the onlookers as complacent and naive — they treat the alien arrival as entertainment, expecting to find something they can understand and control. This complacency reflects broader Victorian attitudes: the belief that Britain was invulnerable and that no force could challenge its supremacy.

Key Fact

Wells sets the invasion in suburban Woking, not an exotic location. The mundane, recognisable setting makes the horror more shocking and forces Victorian readers to imagine the invasion happening to them. The contrast between the ordinary and the extraordinary is a key technique throughout the novel.

Wells reinforces this ordinariness through specific domestic detail. The narrator mentions his wife, his study, his daily routine. He walks to the Common as a curious observer, expecting to see nothing remarkable. This mirrors the attitude of Victorian society as a whole — comfortable, complacent, and utterly unprepared for catastrophe. The genius of Wells’s approach is that he makes the reader share this complacency before shattering it.

Victorian Complacency

The crowd that gathers around the cylinder on Horsell Common behaves as if watching a spectacle. People bring picnic hampers. Boys throw stones. A man sells apples. Wells uses these comic details to satirise the assumption that nothing truly dangerous could happen on English soil. The British Empire had exported violence around the world for centuries, but the homeland itself felt untouchable. The Heat-Ray shatters this illusion in seconds.

The Martians themselves are described with deliberate disgust. The narrator sees “a big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear” with “Gorgon groups of tentacles.” Wells uses the classical reference to Gorgons to link the invasion to mythological horror, suggesting that what the crowd witnesses is beyond rational comprehension. The contrast between the familiar English countryside and the alien horror emerging from the cylinder creates a visceral shock.

The Heat-Ray

When the Martians emerge and deploy the Heat-Ray, the tone shifts violently. The crowd’s curiosity turns to terror. Wells describes people being incinerated in graphic detail: “It was as if each man were suddenly and momentarily turned to fire.” The simile reduces human beings to fuel, stripping away all dignity and individuality. This dehumanisation mirrors how colonial powers described the peoples they conquered.

Wells uses a first-person narrator whose perspective is deliberately limited. He can only report what he personally sees, hears, and feels. This creates uncertainty and suspense — the reader, like the narrator, never has a complete picture of the invasion. It also mimics the experience of real disaster: confusion, fragmented information, and panic.

The narrator’s psychological realism is one of Wells’s most powerful techniques. He admits that his mind kept returning to “the normal” — he expected the army to contain the threat and the government to restore order. This inability to accept the scale of the catastrophe mirrors how real people respond to disasters: with denial, confusion, and a desperate clinging to routine. Wells understood that the greatest obstacle to survival is not external danger but the human refusal to believe that the world has fundamentally changed.

The Collapse of Order

As the Martians advance, Victorian social order rapidly disintegrates. The military fails. Communications break down. Crowds flee in panic. Wells presents this collapse as inevitable — the structures that Victorians relied on (army, police, railways, telegraph) were built to maintain order among humans, not to resist an alien intelligence. The veneer of civilisation is shown to be extraordinarily thin.

Key Fact

The army, police, railways, and telegraph all fail against the Martians. Wells shows that Victorian civilisation is fragile — its institutions depend on unchallenged supremacy. When that supremacy is challenged, everything collapses. This critiques the Victorian belief that their society was permanent and unassailable.

The narrator himself struggles to comprehend what is happening. He admits that his mind kept returning to “the normal” — he expected the army to contain the threat, the government to restore order. This psychological realism is one of Wells’s most powerful techniques. The narrator’s inability to accept the scale of the catastrophe mirrors how real people respond to disasters — with denial, confusion, and a desperate clinging to routine.

Wells devotes significant attention to crowd behaviour during the evacuation. People trample one another, steal food, and abandon the weak. The narrator observes that “the social order” dissolves with terrifying speed. Wells suggests that civilised behaviour is a luxury of safety — when survival is at stake, humans revert to primal instincts. This anticipates twentieth-century psychology and disaster studies.

before.content_html:
The Martian War Machines

As the invasion escalates, the Martians construct towering tripods — colossal three-legged war machines over a hundred feet tall. Wells describes them striding across the landscape with terrifying grace: “monstrous tripods, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees.” The tripods are deliberately designed to be alien and unnatural — three legs instead of four, metal instead of flesh. They represent a technology so advanced that humans cannot comprehend it, let alone fight it.

The Martians also deploy Black Smoke, a chemical weapon that settles over towns and kills all life. Wells may have been anticipating chemical warfare, which would become a horrifying reality in World War I just sixteen years later. The combination of Heat-Ray and Black Smoke makes the Martian assault overwhelmingly one-sided.

Key Fact

The Martians use two weapons: the Heat-Ray (instant incineration, representing superior technology) and Black Smoke (chemical warfare, anticipating WW1 gas attacks). Together, they demonstrate that Victorian military power is utterly outclassed.

The Exodus from London

Wells devotes an entire chapter to the mass evacuation of London, told through the perspective of the narrator’s brother. Six million people flee in chaotic panic. Wells describes the refugee column with devastating precision: families separated, the weak trampled, belongings abandoned. The scene strips away all pretence of Victorian order and decorum. Wealthy and poor alike are reduced to desperate survivors.

Wells uses the brother’s narrative to expand the scope of the evacuation. The brother describes “the roaring wave of fear that swept through the greatest city in the world” — the word “wave” suggests an unstoppable natural force, reducing six million individuals to a single mass of terror. He witnesses acts of both kindness and savagery: strangers help one another, but others steal food, overturn carts, and fight over space on boats. Wells presents humanity without illusions — capable of both compassion and brutality under extreme pressure.

The destruction of HMS Thunder Child is the most dramatic military engagement in the novel. An ironclad warship charges the tripods to protect a fleet of refugee boats. It manages to destroy one tripod before being sunk. Wells makes the scene both heroic and futile — one small victory that changes nothing. The Thunder Child represents the very best of Victorian military technology, and even it is destroyed. This is Wells’s definitive statement: human technology cannot save us.

Wells devotes particular attention to the sounds of the invasion. The tripods emit a chilling “ulla, ulla” cry that haunts the narrator throughout the novel. The Heat-Ray hisses and crackles. The Black Smoke settles silently. Wells uses this auditory landscape to create an atmosphere of alien menace — the sounds are recognisable enough to be terrifying but strange enough to feel utterly inhuman. This sensory detail contributes to the novel’s extraordinary realism, making the fantastical invasion feel viscerally real to the reader.

The Red Weed

As the Martians establish control, a red weed begins spreading across the landscape, choking rivers and covering buildings. The red weed is a powerful symbol of colonisation — just as European settlers introduced their own plants and animals to conquered lands, the Martians are transforming Earth’s environment to suit themselves. The red colour suggests blood, violence, and the total displacement of English nature.

Key Fact

The red weed symbolises colonial transformation: just as European empires introduced their own species to conquered lands, the Martians plant their own vegetation on Earth. The red colour suggests blood and violence. Wells is showing that colonisation does not just kill people — it transforms and erases entire ecosystems.

During the London exodus, the rigid Victorian class system dissolves. Wealthy people abandon their carriages; servants flee without their masters; money becomes meaningless. Wells shows that class distinction is an artificial construct that survives only in stable conditions. When civilisation collapses, all humans are equal in their vulnerability. This is a radical critique of the class system that governed every aspect of Victorian life.

Wells’s Prophetic Vision

Many elements of Book 1 proved eerily prophetic. The Black Smoke anticipated the poison gas attacks of World War I (1914–1918). The mass evacuation of London foreshadowed the real evacuations of World War II. The collapse of communication and infrastructure mirrors modern disaster scenarios. Wells was not predicting the future in detail, but he understood something fundamental: that technologically advanced societies are more fragile than they appear, because their complexity makes them vulnerable to disruption.

The destruction of HMS Thunder Child is particularly resonant. The warship represents the absolute pinnacle of Victorian military engineering — an ironclad, steam-powered vessel bristling with guns. Its heroic charge against the tripods is one of the novel’s most dramatic set-pieces. But the outcome is devastating: the Thunder Child destroys one tripod but is then overwhelmed. Wells uses this scene to argue that even the greatest achievements of human engineering are finite. Against a truly superior force, courage and technology are not enough.

before.content_html:
Book 2: The Earth Under the Martians

Book 2 shifts from large-scale warfare to intimate survival horror. The narrator is trapped in a ruined house with the curate, directly adjacent to a Martian pit. For days they hide, ration food, and listen to the Martians operating their machinery. Wells uses this confined setting to explore how extreme stress strips away civilised behaviour. The curate, a man of God, becomes hysterical and selfish, hoarding food and screaming. The narrator is forced to knock him unconscious to prevent the Martians from hearing them.

The curate’s collapse is morally complex. He is not a villain but a man whose entire worldview — his faith that God controls events and protects the righteous — has been destroyed. He wails “Why are these things permitted?” and “What are these Martians? … What has God wrought?” Wells uses the curate to explore what happens when faith is tested by genuine catastrophe. The curate’s religion provides no practical survival skills and, worse, his self-pity and noise endanger both their lives. When the narrator finally strikes him, it is an act of pragmatic necessity that Wells uses to show how survival demands a harder morality than peacetime allows.

Key Fact

The curate represents the failure of organised religion under crisis. He is selfish, irrational, and hysterical when faith is tested by real danger. Wells — an atheist — uses the curate to argue that religious institutions provide no genuine moral strength when civilisation collapses.

The Artilleryman

After escaping the ruined house, the narrator encounters the artilleryman, who outlines a vision for rebuilding humanity underground. He talks of creating a new civilisation, breeding strong people, and fighting back. His speech is compelling but ultimately hollow — when the narrator visits his “tunnel,” it is barely started. The artilleryman represents rhetoric without action — all talk and no work.

The artilleryman’s vision has a darker edge. He talks about creating a new civilisation of “strong and sane” people, selecting who deserves to survive. This echoes the eugenic thinking that was gaining popularity in Victorian Britain. Wells presents the artilleryman sympathetically at first — his ideas sound bold and practical — but then reveals them as fantasies. The barely-started tunnel exposes the gap between words and deeds. This is Wells’s satire of the kind of person who responds to crisis with grandiose plans but lacks the discipline to implement them.

In one of the novel’s most disturbing revelations, the narrator discovers that the Martians feed by injecting human blood directly into their own veins. This makes humans literal livestock — a horrifying inversion of the human-animal relationship. Wells forces the reader to experience what it feels like to be treated as a resource rather than a sentient being, directly paralleling the colonial treatment of indigenous peoples.

The Martians’ Defeat

The novel’s resolution is one of the most famous in literature. The Martians are not defeated by human weapons, intelligence, or courage — they are killed by bacteria. Earth’s common germs, to which humans have long been immune through millennia of evolution, prove fatal to the Martians. Wells writes that they were “slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth.”

This ending is deeply significant. It rejects the idea that humanity is saved by heroism or technology. Instead, it is biology — the same Darwinian process that produced the Martians — that saves us. Wells is also referencing the real history of colonisation: European diseases killed vast numbers of indigenous peoples in the Americas. The bacteria ending mirrors this history, completing the colonial reversal.

The phrase “the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth” carries multiple layers of meaning. The word “humblest” undercuts human pride — it is not human intelligence, bravery, or technology that saves the species, but microscopic organisms. The reference to “God” is ironic given the curate’s failure of faith; Wells suggests that if there is a divine plan, it operates through biological processes rather than supernatural intervention. The phrase also implies humility — that humanity should be humble about its place in the natural order.

Key Fact

Wells chose bacteria to reject the idea that heroism or technology saves humanity. The Darwinian ending shows that survival depends on evolution, not military power. It also mirrors colonial history: European diseases devastated indigenous peoples, and now Earth’s germs devastate the colonising Martians.

The novel ends with the narrator reflecting on the invasion’s legacy. He suggests that the experience has permanently changed humanity’s view of itself: “We can never regard this earth as the entire universe, or regard any creature of its own in the same way we did before.” The invasion has destroyed human exceptionalism. Wells leaves the reader with a sense of ongoing vulnerability — the Martians could return at any time.

before.content_html:
Characters & Narration

Unlike most novels, The War of the Worlds has very few developed characters. The narrator is unnamed, the secondary characters are types rather than individuals, and the Martians are described in biological rather than psychological terms. This is deliberate. Wells is not writing a character study — he is writing a speculative parable about what would happen if Britain’s imperial assumptions were challenged. The characters serve the argument, not the other way around.

The Narrator

The unnamed narrator is a middle-class writer and “professed student of philosophy” living in Woking. His ordinariness is important — he is an Everyman figure. His scientific education allows him to observe and analyse the Martians, but his emotional responses are entirely human: fear, confusion, despair, and ultimately a cautious hope. Wells uses his limited perspective to create uncertainty and suspense.

Key Fact

The unnamed narrator is an Everyman figure — his ordinariness allows the reader to identify with him and imagine themselves in the invasion. His scientific background enables analysis, but his emotional responses are universal: fear, confusion, and despair.

The narrator writes his account retrospectively — he is looking back on events that have already happened. This creates a tension between the terrified man living through the invasion and the calmer, more analytical voice reflecting on it afterwards. Wells uses this dual perspective to combine the immediacy of first-person experience with the authority of hindsight. The narrator occasionally references events he could not have witnessed directly, explaining that he learned about them later from his brother or from published accounts. This journalistic approach adds verisimilitude — it feels like a genuine testimony rather than a neat fictional narrative.

Crucially, the narrator is morally ambiguous. He kills the curate (or at least strikes him unconscious, leading to his death). He struggles with cowardice, hiding underground rather than fighting. He is not a hero but an ordinary man doing what he must to survive. Wells deliberately avoids creating a traditional protagonist — there is no climactic battle, no clever plan to defeat the aliens. The narrator simply endures. This is a radical choice for Victorian fiction, which typically celebrated heroic individualism.

The Artilleryman

The artilleryman appears twice: first as a shell-shocked survivor, then as a self-appointed visionary. His second appearance is more significant. He outlines grandiose plans for rebuilding civilisation underground, selecting the “strong and sane” to survive. His rhetoric echoes Social Darwinist ideas about the survival of the fittest. But his tunnel is barely started. Wells uses him as a satire of people who respond to crisis with big talk and no action.

The artilleryman’s rhetoric also reveals a disturbing authoritarianism. He talks about selecting who is “worth” saving, dividing humanity into the strong and the weak. This echoes Social Darwinist thinking and anticipates the eugenics movement that would gain influence in the early twentieth century. Wells — who himself held complicated views on eugenics — presents these ideas with enough surface appeal to show how seductive they can be, before exposing their hollowness through the artilleryman’s failure to act on them.

The curate breaks down completely under the stress of the invasion. He quotes scripture obsessively, hoards food, and becomes a danger to the narrator’s survival. Wells, an atheist, uses the curate to argue that religious faith, when not backed by genuine moral character, collapses under pressure. The curate is a contrast with the narrator, who survives through practical reason rather than faith.

The Martians as Characters

The Martians are described in purely biological terms: large brains, no digestive systems, reproducing by budding. Wells deliberately avoids giving them personalities or motivations beyond survival. They are a narrative force rather than characters. This makes them more terrifying — they cannot be reasoned with, negotiated with, or appealed to. They treat humans with the same indifference that humans show to insects.

Key Fact

Wells describes the Martians biologically (brains, tentacles, budding reproduction) to remove any possibility of communication or empathy. They are a force of nature, not villains. This makes them more terrifying and reinforces the Darwinian theme: survival is about biology, not morality.

The narrator’s brother provides a second perspective on the invasion, describing the London exodus. This dual viewpoint expands the novel’s scope without breaking the first-person framework. Wells uses the brother to show events the narrator could not witness, while maintaining the subjective, limited feel of eyewitness testimony.

Character as Function

In traditional Victorian novels, characters are developed through dialogue, backstory, and psychological insight. Wells does almost none of this. The narrator has no name. The curate and artilleryman are defined by their social roles, not their personalities. The Martians have no individual identity at all. This is deliberate: Wells is writing an allegory, not a character study. Each figure represents a type of response to catastrophe: practical endurance (narrator), religious collapse (curate), empty rhetoric (artilleryman). Understanding this principle is essential for AO2 analysis in the Eduqas exam.

before.content_html:
Science Fiction as Social Commentary

Wells is often called the “father of science fiction.” But his science fiction is never purely about aliens or technology — it is always about society. The Martians are a thought experiment: what happens when the logic of imperialism is applied to Britain itself? The Heat-Ray, Black Smoke, and tripods are not just exciting inventions — they are tools for examining human vulnerability, arrogance, and the fragility of civilisation.

Key Fact

Wells uses alien invasion not as adventure but as critique. The Martians represent British imperialism reversed; the Heat-Ray exposes technological overconfidence; the bacteria ending reinforces Darwinian evolution over human heroism. Every science fiction element serves a social argument.

Wells was part of a broader literary tradition. Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) and Robert Louis Stevenson’s Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886) had already used fantastic scenarios to explore real anxieties. But Wells took the genre further by grounding his fiction in real science. Where Shelley used vague galvanism, Wells based his Martians on genuine evolutionary biology. This scientific rigour makes the novel feel more plausible and the social critique more powerful — the reader cannot dismiss the Martians as mere fantasy when they operate according to recognisable Darwinian principles.

The Two-Book Structure

The novel is divided into two books: Book 1: The Coming of the Martians (large-scale invasion, military response, societal collapse) and Book 2: The Earth Under the Martians (personal survival, underground hiding, encounters with curate and artilleryman, resolution). This structural division shifts the focus from the public to the private, from spectacle to psychology.

Book 1 is fast-paced: invasion, battles, exodus. Book 2 slows dramatically: the narrator is trapped, hiding, rationing food. This change of pace creates a claustrophobic, psychological tension very different from the action of Book 1. Wells shows that survival is not exciting — it is tedious, terrifying, and morally corrosive.

Within each book, Wells also uses structural patterns to reinforce his argument. Book 1 follows a rhythm of escalation: each chapter introduces a greater threat (cylinder, Heat-Ray, tripods, Black Smoke, exodus). This relentless escalation creates the sense that events are spiralling out of control. Book 2 follows a rhythm of contraction: the narrator’s world shrinks from Surrey to a ruined house to a single room. This structural mirror — one expanding, one contracting — reflects the novel’s movement from public crisis to private survival.

The novel’s resolution also has structural significance. The Martians die suddenly, without warning, in the middle of a chapter. There is no climactic battle, no final confrontation. Wells deliberately denies the reader the satisfaction of a dramatic ending. This anti-climax is itself a statement: survival in the real world is not a story with a satisfying arc. It is messy, arbitrary, and unglamorous.

The Retrospective Frame

The narrator writes his account after the invasion has ended. This retrospective framing creates a dual perspective: the terrified man living through events and the calmer voice reflecting on them afterwards. Wells uses this to combine the terror of immediate experience with the analytical authority of hindsight. The narrator says “I did not know then what I know now” — building tension while adding credibility. This technique also allows Wells to incorporate information the narrator learned later, such as events witnessed by his brother in London, without breaking the first-person framework.

Narrative Techniques

Wells uses several distinctive techniques: (1) journalistic register — the narrator writes as if documenting events, using precise dates, locations, and measurements. (2) direct address — the narrator occasionally speaks directly to the reader (“the reader will remember”). (3) Scientific language — the Martians are described with biological precision, not emotional language.

Key Fact

Three techniques: (1) Journalistic register creates realism and authority. (2) Direct address involves the reader personally. (3) Scientific language for the Martians removes emotion and reinforces the Darwinian framework.

The narrator admits he cannot always be trusted. He was exhausted, terrified, and sometimes delirious. Wells uses this unreliability to replicate the experience of living through disaster: information is fragmented, contradictory, and incomplete. The reader, like the narrator, must piece together what is happening from incomplete evidence.

Wells’s Legacy

The War of the Worlds established many of the conventions that science fiction still uses today: the alien invasion, the destruction of familiar landmarks, the collapse of civilisation, and the survivor narrative. But Wells’s greatest achievement was demonstrating that science fiction could be serious literature — not escapist fantasy but a powerful tool for examining real social and political issues. For the Eduqas exam, understanding Wells’s pioneering role in the genre helps you analyse how he uses its conventions to serve his argument about empire, evolution, and the fragility of human civilisation. His influence extends through Orwell, Wyndham, and modern science fiction — but unlike many of his followers, Wells never lost sight of the social purpose behind the spectacle.

before.content_html:
Key Themes

The five most important themes in The War of the Worlds for the Eduqas exam are: imperialism and colonisation, evolution and survival, the fragility of civilisation, the limits of technology, and humanity’s place in the universe.

Imperialism & Colonisation

The novel’s central argument is a reversal of imperialism. The Martians treat humans exactly as the British treated colonised peoples: conquering territory, extracting resources (blood), and transforming the environment (red weed). Wells makes this parallel explicit with the Tasmanian reference. The entire invasion is a thought experiment: what if the most powerful empire on Earth experienced what it had done to others?

This colonial critique operates on multiple levels. The Martians conquer territory (Surrey, London), extract resources (human blood for feeding), and transform the environment (the red weed displacing English vegetation). Each of these mirrors a specific aspect of British imperialism. Wells also shows how colonisation dehumanises both the coloniser and the colonised. The Martians treat humans with clinical indifference — the same indifference that British administrators showed towards the peoples they governed. By forcing his readers to experience this indifference as victims, Wells creates empathy for the colonised world.

Key Fact

The Martians colonise Britain as Britain colonised others: military conquest, resource extraction (human blood), environmental transformation (red weed). Wells’s opening reference to the Tasmanian genocide makes the parallel explicit.

Evolution & Survival

Darwinism underpins the entire novel. The Martians are a more evolved species applying the logic of natural selection. The bacteria ending shows that survival depends on biological adaptation, not heroism or technology. Wells challenges human exceptionalism — we are one species among many, vulnerable to extinction.

The Darwinian framework is consistent throughout the novel. The Martians are described in purely biological terms: large brains, atrophied digestive systems, reproduction by budding rather than sexual intercourse. They represent what humanity might become after millions of years of further evolution — pure intellect without emotion. Wells studied under Huxley and understood evolution as an ongoing, amoral process. The bacteria ending is the ultimate Darwinian statement: survival depends on adaptation, not superiority. The Martians, despite their intelligence, lack one crucial adaptation — immunity to Earth’s microbes — and this kills them.

Victorian society prided itself on progress, order, and stability. Wells shows how quickly these collapse: the army fails, the class system dissolves, crowds become mobs, religious faith crumbles. The message is that civilisation is not permanent or guaranteed — it depends on conditions that can be destroyed overnight. This theme resonated powerfully in the early twentieth century as two World Wars proved Wells right.

Understanding these thematic interconnections allows you to write more sophisticated exam responses. Rather than discussing themes in isolation, the strongest candidates weave multiple themes together in every paragraph, showing how Wells constructs a unified argument about humanity’s vulnerability, the moral bankruptcy of empire, and the humbling power of natural forces beyond human control.

The Limits of Technology

Victorians worshipped technological progress — railways, telegraphs, steam engines, and warships seemed to prove human mastery over nature. Wells systematically destroys this confidence. The artillery fails. HMS Thunder Child is sunk. Communication networks break down. Even the Martians’ superior technology ultimately fails — killed by something technology cannot control: bacteria. The message is that technology is a tool, not a salvation.

Wells extends this critique beyond military technology. The telegraph and railway — the communication and transport networks that held the Empire together — are among the first systems to fail. Newspapers stop printing. Trains stop running. Without these systems, Victorian society cannot coordinate a response. Wells understood that advanced societies are fragile precisely because they are complex: the more interconnected a system is, the more catastrophically it fails when disrupted. This insight feels remarkably modern — it anticipates twenty-first-century concerns about infrastructure vulnerability and systemic risk.

Key Fact

Both human and Martian technology fail. Human weapons cannot stop the Heat-Ray. Martian technology cannot prevent death by bacteria. Wells argues that technology is always limited — evolution (biology) is more powerful than invention (engineering).

The novel ends with the narrator reflecting that humanity can “never regard this earth as the entire universe” again. The invasion has permanently changed human self-perception. We are not the centre of creation but one vulnerable species in a vast, indifferent cosmos. This anticipates the existential anxiety of the twentieth century and makes the novel feel startlingly modern.

Linking Themes for the Exam

In the Eduqas exam, the strongest responses will connect themes rather than treating them in isolation. For example, imperialism and evolution are linked because Social Darwinism was used to justify the Empire. The fragility of civilisation and the limits of technology are linked because Victorian confidence rested on both social institutions and engineering achievements. Humanity’s place in the universe connects all the other themes: the novel argues that we are not exceptional, not invulnerable, and not the pinnacle of creation. Every theme contributes to this central argument about humility.

before.description: Eduqas Component 2 Section B exam technique for the War of the Worlds extract question.
before.content_html:
19th-Century Novel Exam Technique: The War of the Worlds

19th-century novel questions typically give you a printed extract from the text and ask you to write about its significance and its importance in the novel as a whole. Your answer is marked against the Assessment Objectives: AO1 (critical response with textual references), AO2 (analysis of language, form and structure), AO3 (understanding of context), and on some boards AO4 (accuracy of written expression). Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark allocation and which AOs are assessed on your paper.

Key Fact

AO1: Critical response with textual references. AO2: Analysis of language, form, structure. AO3: Context. AO4: Accuracy of expression. The strongest paragraphs show evidence of more than one AO at a time.

On any paper where context is assessed, your understanding of Victorian imperialism, Darwinism, class, and science is just as important as your analysis of Wells’s language techniques. Where written accuracy is assessed, careless spelling, punctuation, and grammar will cost you marks. Use literary terminology accurately: words like “semantic field,” “pathetic fallacy,” “motif,” and “narrative perspective” demonstrate sophisticated analysis and strengthen AO2 (and, where assessed, AO4).

Key Extracts to Prepare

The richest passages for analysis: (1) The opening chapter with Tasmanian reference. (2) The Heat-Ray scene on Horsell Common. (3) The London exodus. (4) HMS Thunder Child’s destruction. (5) The narrator trapped with the curate. (6) The bacteria ending.

For each passage, prepare at least three analytical points covering different AOs. For the opening chapter, you might analyse: (1) the Tasmanian reference and its colonial critique (AO3), (2) the calm, scientific register that contrasts with the horror to come (AO2), and (3) the retrospective framing that creates dramatic irony (AO2). For the bacteria ending: (1) the anti-climactic resolution rejecting heroic conventions (AO2), (2) “the humblest things” as an ironic commentary on human pride (AO2), and (3) the Darwinian logic that mirrors colonial disease history (AO3).

Use: “Wells uses [technique] to present [idea], reflecting [context]. The effect on the reader is [impact]. This connects to the wider novel because [link].” This ensures every paragraph addresses AO1 (reference), AO2 (method), AO3 (context), and is expressed clearly (AO4).

Time Management

Work out in advance how long you can afford to spend on this question and split the time between reading and planning, writing, and proofreading. A useful rule of thumb is to plan 3–4 key points before you start writing, and to leave at least 5 minutes at the end to proofread. Each point should cover the extract AND the wider text.

A good plan identifies your key points and the quotations you will use for each. Write short bullet points, not full sentences. For example: “Point 1: colonial parallel — Tasmanian reference, ‘inferior races’, red weed as territorial claim. Link to wider: blood feeding, Thunder Child = futility. Context: British Empire, Social Darwinism.” This plan takes under a minute to write but ensures your response is structured and addresses several AOs.

Model Paragraph Structure

The strongest paragraphs integrate several AOs naturally. Begin with a clear analytical point about the extract (AO1). Analyse Wells’s specific technique — a word choice, structural feature, or narrative device (AO2). Link this to a contextual factor such as imperialism, Darwinism, or Victorian class (AO3). Ensure the whole paragraph is expressed in clear, grammatically accurate English using literary terminology (AO4). A useful sentence scaffold: “Wells uses [technique] to present [idea/character], reflecting [context], which forces the reader to [response].”

Common Mistakes

Avoid: (1) Retelling the plot instead of analysing Wells’s methods. (2) Only discussing the extract without connecting to the wider novel. (3) Listing context (“The British Empire existed”) without linking to purpose. (4) Ignoring accuracy — clear expression is always rewarded and, on some boards, explicitly marked. (5) Not using literary terminology.

Another common weakness is treating the extract in isolation. A strong response always connects outward to other parts of the text. If your extract is from Book 1, discuss how the events connect to Book 2. If it features the narrator, compare his perspective with the curate’s or the artilleryman’s. If it describes the Martians, connect to the opening chapter’s colonial framework and the bacteria ending. This demonstrates the sustained critical style that examiners reward at the highest bands.

Key Fact

Three AO2 methods: (1) First-person limited narrator creating suspense and uncertainty. (2) Journalistic register for realism. (3) Scientific biological language for the Martians, removing emotion and reinforcing the Darwinian framework.

Good context integration: “Wells references the Tasmanian genocide to force Victorian readers to see the invasion from the perspective of colonised peoples, critiquing the imperial arrogance that underpinned the British Empire.” Bad: “The British Empire controlled a quarter of the world.” Always link context to method AND purpose.

AO4: Quality of Expression

Where AO4 is assessed, it is often underestimated. Write in formal academic register. Avoid slang, contractions, and informal phrases like “this shows that.” Instead, use precise analytical vocabulary: “Wells employs,” “this reinforces,” “the reader is compelled to.” Proofread your final response — check for comma splices, run-on sentences, and common misspellings of literary terms. Strong written expression also means structuring your paragraphs logically, with each one making a distinct point rather than repeating earlier ideas.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • 40 marks split equally across AO1, AO2, AO3, AO4. Always write about extract AND wider text.
  • Prepare six high-value passages; use the paragraph scaffold to integrate all AOs.
  • Avoid retelling, context-listing, and ignoring AO4. Use literary terminology and proofread.
